title: Can anger be a good thing?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether anger can be beneficial. They open with Incredible Hulk and Bruce Banner as a comparison, then cite a survey where 28 percent of people viewed their own anger as bad, and an Aristotle quote on being angry at the right things, with the right people, in the right way. They cover three reasons people get angry (correcting bad behavior, demonstrating power, addressing interpersonal conflict), a women's anger study and anger triggers (women angered by those close to them, men by strangers), the amygdala and frontal lobe "wrestling match" in the brain, Phineas Gage's frontal lobe injury, gender differences in anger expression, and a Santa Barbara study finding angry people better at spotting weak arguments. They close that suppressing anger is unhealthy and that the key is expressing it appropriately. The episode ends with listener mail from Adam Asher about a video game possibly titled MK Ultra, following up on an earlier episode about the CIA LSD program.

segments.title: Opening banter and The Incredible Hulk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck greet listeners and reminisce about The Incredible Hulk, with Bruce Banner's anger transformations, which Josh uses as a segue into the idea that anger can be beneficial.

segments.title: Anger can be beneficial
segments.summary: Josh says people tend to see anger as bad, citing a survey where 28 percent of respondents called their own anger bad. Chuck argues anger is appropriate. They discuss gentility in society and an Aristotle quote on being angry at the right things and in the right way.

segments.title: Reasons people get angry
segments.summary: They describe three reasons people get angry: to correct others' bad behavior, to demonstrate power, and to address interpersonal conflict, which Josh frames as a kind gesture when done constructively.

segments.title: Women's anger study and anger triggers
segments.summary: Josh cites a women's anger study finding powerlessness, injustice and others' irresponsibility as top roots of women's anger. They discuss anger triggers, which tend to involve people close to women and strangers for men. Chuck describes road rage in Atlanta's carpool lane.

segments.title: Brain wrestling: amygdala and frontal lobe
segments.summary: Josh explains that anger triggers a contest between the amygdala, which handles emotion, and the frontal lobe, which handles reason, lasting about two seconds, with the frontal lobe usually winning. They discuss a hot-tempered classmate and an acquaintance in Arizona.

segments.title: Phineas Gage
segments.summary: Josh describes Phineas Gage, a railroad worker whose frontal lobe was damaged by an iron rod through his head, leaving him a changed, angrier man while his amygdala was intact.

segments.title: Gender differences in anger expression
segments.summary: They review a study finding men scored higher on physical and passive aggression and revenge motives, while women stayed angry longer, were more resentful, and used indirect aggression such as cutting off people.

segments.title: Santa Barbara study: anger and analytical skills
segments.summary: Two psychologists had students angered or kept neutral, then evaluated essays. The angry students were better at distinguishing well-supported arguments from flowery but weak ones. They suggest anger focuses attention and motivates punishing poor work.

segments.title: Channeling anger and suppression
segments.summary: Chuck concludes the key is to channel anger into positivity. They note studies linking suppressed anger to higher mortality, while physical aggression is harmful, so the goal is expressing anger the right way.

segments.title: Listener mail: MK Ultra video game
segments.summary: Listener Adam Asher recalls a video game possibly called MK Ultra featuring a costumed man with a gun for an arm and a talking dog, and asks whether it exists. The hosts ask listeners for details and close with the usual plugs.
